author: Vitor
notes: This was one hell of a climb, but so rewarding to get a first-try pass, even if a TLE.
aiExplanation: This function simulates **k servers** handling incoming requests to find which servers end up handling the most. It keeps a min-priority queue called `busy` ordered by the time each server finishes its current job, a `dp` array counting how many requests each server handled, and an `attributed` array marking which servers are currently occupied. The first `min(k, n)` requests are assigned directly to servers `0..k-1`, since every server starts free. For each later request, the loop first dequeues every server whose finish time is at or before the current `arrival` time and marks it free again. If any server is free, it scans forward from index `i % k`, wrapping around with `(i + j) % k`, and picks the first unoccupied one, increments its count, and pushes its new finish time (`time + load[i]`) into the queue; if no server is free, the request is simply dropped. Finally it finds the maximum count in `dp` and returns every server index that reached it. The weakness is the linear scan for a free server inside the main loop, which makes the worst case **O(n · k)** and is why this submission hit the time limit.

author: Leetcode
notes: By looking at this code, one gets the (wrong) sense that this exercise isn't all that hard.
aiExplanation: This is the same simulation, but it uses **two priority queues** so that finding the next available server is logarithmic instead of linear. The `free` queue holds the indices of idle servers, initially all of `0..k-1`, while `busy` holds `[finish time, server]` pairs ordered by finish time. For each request `i` arriving at time `t`, it first moves every server whose finish time is `<= t` from `busy` back into `free`. The clever part is the key used when re-inserting: `i + (x - i % k + k) % k` computes the first index at or after `i` that maps to server `x` modulo `k`, so popping the smallest key from `free` yields exactly the server a round-robin scan starting at `i % k` would pick, and taking that key `% k` recovers the server id. If no server is free the request is dropped with `continue`; otherwise the chosen server is pushed into `busy` with finish time `t + load[i]` and its `handled` count is incremented. At the end it finds the maximum in `handled` with `reduce` and returns every server index whose count equals that maximum.
